Cerebral Palsy

early signs · the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pattern names the cause · periventricular leukomalacia · stroke, asphyxia, infection · spinal mimicsWhat does the MRI actually describe, and are the findings unilateral or global?

Source vignette Pt — 7 mo, born at 31 weeks, left-sided spasticity · Imaging — MRI shows white matter injury beside the right lateral ventricle · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned ischemic injury of the periventricular white matter of prematurity, transplacental Toxoplasma infection and inherited thrombophilia with perinatal stroke
The decision point

White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia. It is ischemia and necrosis in the poorly perfused zone beside the ventricles, and the signature injury of prematurity. The examination independently confirms a unilateral injury. Increased tone, 3+ reflexes and ankle clonus on the left only, with a right-sided lesion, is spastic hemiplegia. A congenital infection produces global deficits, not one-sided spasticity.

Defining criteria Cerebral palsy — nonprogressive motor dysfunction caused by a neurologic injury; the etiology is often multifactorial and may never be identified · Periventricular leukomalacia — ischemia and necrosis of the poorly perfused white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles, seen as white matter injury on MRI; premature infants are at greatest risk, and their friable germinal matrix vessels also predispose to intraventricular hemorrhage · Early signs that should raise suspicion — motor delay (not rolling by 4 months corrected), early hand preference before age 1, persistent neonatal reflexes (tonic neck beyond 6 months), abnormal tone · The tone evolution — infants may be hypotonic initially, with spasticity developing over time, accompanied by hyperreflexia and often clonus
Pertinent positives & negatives White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle — periventricular leukomalacia, which points to prematurity; each other cause has a different imaging signature · Born at 31 weeks — prematurity is a significant risk factor for cerebral palsy · Left-sided findings with a right-sided lesion — spastic hemiplegia matching a unilateral injury; intrauterine infection produces global, not one-sided, deficits · Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, sustained clonus — upper motor neuron; excludes spinal dysraphism, where lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased · Early hand preference at 7 months — abnormal before age 1, and one of the earliest signs · Not rolling over — motor delay, judged against corrected age in a 31-weeker · Head circumference at the 50th percentile — no microcephaly, which argues further against congenital infection · Babinski present bilaterally — normal up to 24 months only in an otherwise normal examination; the abnormal sign is the asymmetry of tone and reflexes · Veterinary office, inconsistent prenatal care — suggest toxoplasmosis, but the MRI pattern refutes it
Cerebral palsy: the MRI pattern names the cause
EtiologyIllness scriptThe National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tell: imagingExcluded here by
Prematurity / low birth weightIschemia in the watershed white matter beside the ventricles; friable germinal matrix vesselsPeriventricular leukomalacia; intraventricular hemorrhage(the answer)
Hypoxic-ischemic injuryPerinatal asphyxia in a term infant; low Apgars, encephalopathy, seizuresWatershed injury; basal ganglia and thalamic lesionsBorn preterm; no depressed Apgars or neonatal encephalopathy described
Perinatal stroke (± inherited thrombophilia)Arterial infarct around the time of birth; hemiplegia emerging in infancyInfarct in a vascular distribution, most often the middle cerebral arteryThe lesion is periventricular white matter, not a territory
Intrauterine infectionCytomegalovirus (CMV), toxoplasmosis; transplacental transmissionIntracranial calcifications; microcephaly; global deficitsPeriventricular white matter injury, normocephaly, unilateral findings
Neural tube defect (folate deficiency)Spinal dysraphismA spinal lesion, and the examination is lower motor neuron: decreased lower-extremity tone and reflexesHypertonia with hyperreflexia and clonus
Magnesium sulfate exposureGiven to the mother for preterm laborTransient neonatal hypotonia onlyFindings at 7 months, and they are hypertonic
Management, in one line Cerebral palsy is managed supportively and lifelong. Care includes early intervention and physical therapy, tone management, and surveillance of hips, feeding and growth, and seizures, with vision and hearing evaluation. No treatment reverses the static injury itself.
Decision spine Upper or lower motor neuron? — Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, clonus → upper · Unilateral or global? — Left side only → a single-sided lesion, so global insults are excluded · What does the MRI actually say? — Periventricular white matter → leukomalacia · What produces that pattern? — Prematurity; she was born at 31 weeks · Does any exposure in the history produce it? — No: infection calcifies, thrombophilia infarcts a territory, magnesium is transient, folate affects the spine

TestOrderResultWhat it points to

Scenario bank
  1. 7 mo born at 31 weeks with left-sided spasticity and MRI showing white matter injury beside the right lateral ventricle → Ischemic injury of the periventricular white matter of prematurity → Periventricular leukomalacia
  2. Term infant with Apgars 2 and 4, neonatal encephalopathy and seizures; MRI shows watershed and basal ganglia lesions → Hypoxic-ischemic injury → The term-infant pattern
  3. 4 mo term infant with new left arm weakness; MRI shows infarct in the right middle cerebral artery territory → Evaluate for perinatal stroke risk factors including thrombophilia → A vascular distribution, not leukomalacia
  4. Newborn with microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss and petechiae → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → Calcifications rather than white matter injury
  5. 7 mo infant with early hand preference and asymmetric tone, growing normally → Refer for brain MRI and early intervention therapy → Suspected cerebral palsy
  6. 3 yo with spastic diplegia, toe-walking and tight hamstrings, ambulating with difficulty → Physical therapy with orthoses and focal tone management → The commonest cerebral palsy subtype
  7. 7 mo infant born at 31 weeks who is not yet rolling; parents ask whether she is delayed → Assess milestones against her corrected age of about 5 months → Correct the age before judging delay
  8. 6 mo infant with decreased lower-extremity tone, absent reflexes and a sacral dimple → Spinal imaging → Closed spinal dysraphism
  9. 4 yo with known cerebral palsy who has lost independent ambulation over 6 months → Attributing the regression to the cerebral palsy → Cerebral palsy is nonprogressive
  10. 5 yo with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy at a routine health maintenance visit → Hip surveillance imaging with feeding, growth, vision, hearing and seizure review → The comorbidities of a static injury
  11. 2 yo M, term, hypotonic at 4 months and sitting only at 10 months; over the past 3 months has developed spasticity and dystonia with involuntary hand and foot movements, and for the past month bites his fingers and hands, pinches himself and bangs his limbs; family history unremarkable; nonverbal; hypertonia, hyperreflexia and bilateral extensor plantar responses; new and healing abrasions on the fingers and hands → Lesch-Nyhan syndrome → HGPRT deficiency; check serum uric acid
  12. 2 yo F who babbled, reached for toys and said a few words by 12 months, then over 6 months stopped speaking and using her hands purposefully; now makes constant hand-wringing movements; head growth has slowed from the 50th to the 10th percentile → Rett syndrome → MECP2 testing; regression is not consistent with cerebral palsy
Decoy note The veterinary office evokes cat litter, and the inconsistent prenatal care reinforces it, but the MRI refutes it. Of the three maternal drugs named, the antenatal corticosteroids actually lowered this infant's risk rather than raising it. The asymmetry of tone and reflexes is the abnormal sign.
Pearls White matter injury beside the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia, and prematurity is what causes it. · The imaging pattern maps to the insult: periventricular white matter → prematurity · watershed or basal ganglia → hypoxic-ischemic injury · a vascular territory → perinatal stroke · calcifications → congenital infection. · Distribution defines the subtype: both legs is spastic diplegia, the commonest; one side is spastic hemiplegia, which should match a unilateral lesion. · Hand preference before age 1 is abnormal, and it is often the earliest sign a parent reports. · Cerebral palsy is nonprogressive; losing an acquired milestone is not consistent with cerebral palsy and reopens the workup. · Infants with cerebral palsy may begin hypotonic and become spastic later, so normal early tone never excludes it. · Magnesium sulfate given before anticipated early preterm birth is neuroprotective and reduces cerebral palsy risk in surviving infants.
When it is not cerebral palsy Lesch-Nyhan syndrome — a boy who is hypotonic and delayed in infancy, then by about age 3 develops new dystonia, spasticity and hyperreflexia and self-mutilation (biting fingers and hands, banging limbs); X-linked recessive HGPRT deficiency (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) with high uric acid, and gouty arthritis and obstructive nephropathy later if untreated · Rett syndrome — a girl with normal early development who regresses after about 6 months, losing speech and purposeful hand use, with hand wringing · Autism spectrum disorder — social and language deficits, sometimes self-injury, but no spasticity, dystonia or pyramidal signs · Progression — cerebral palsy is nonprogressive, so new movement signs or self-injury after a hypotonic infancy mean a progressive or metabolic disease
Pairs with Part II Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant covers periventricular leukomalacia and intraventricular hemorrhage as prematurity outcomes, and the corrected-age arithmetic this brief uses. Part II Congenital Infections (TORCH) covers the calcification pattern and the global-deficit picture, which is where toxoplasmosis belongs. Part II Spinal Dysraphism covers the upper-versus-lower motor neuron examination that separates a brain lesion from a spinal one. Part I Tics and Tic Disorders covers Tourette syndrome, and Part I Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth covers the regression red flags. Ask: what does the imaging actually describe, and are the deficits one-sided or global? Part I Hypotonia in an Infant covers the floppy infant before any spasticity appears: is the problem in the brain or the motor unit? Part II Imprinting Disorders: Angelman and Prader-Willi separates Rett syndrome from Angelman syndrome. Ask: did the child lose skills, or never gain them?
Transferable rule An exposure in the history suggests a cause; only a described imaging pattern decides it. When a stem gives both, read the imaging first.
Salient decoyTransplacental Toxoplasma gondii: Congenital infection produces intracranial calcifications and global deficits; this MRI describes periventricular white matter and the findings are strictly one-sided, in a normocephalic infant
True-fact-wrong-slotLack of maternal folic acid: Folate deficiency causes neural tube defects, in which lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased, the opposite of this examination
Unchecked attributeMaternal magnesium sulfate: It causes transient hypotonia in the immediate newborn period, not lasting spasticity at 7 months
Class-vs-memberInherited thrombophilia: Stroke shows an infarct in a vascular distribution, usually the middle cerebral artery, not periventricular leukomalacia

Congenital Hypothyroidism

newborn screen · thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) direction locates the defect · goiter or none · dysgenesis as the default · treat before imagingIs TSH high or low, and is there a goiter?

Source vignette Pt — 1 mo old, home birth with no newborn screen, sleepy and feeding poorly, jaundiced since the first week, large tongue; no goiter described, maternal diet balanced with prenatal vitamins · Labs — TSH 110, thyroxine (T4) 0.6 · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, iodine deficiency, panhypopituitarism and neonatal Graves disease
The decision point

TSH 110 with T4 0.6 (TSH, thyroid-stimulating hormone; T4, thyroxine) puts the lesion below the pituitary. The feedback loop is intact, so panhypopituitarism is excluded outright. Neonatal Graves gives a suppressed TSH with high T4, so it is excluded in the opposite direction. Among the primary causes, the exam is silent on goiter and the maternal history is clean (balanced diet, prenatal vitamins). This removes the tell of the two goitrous causes, dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency. The default remains: dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland arrested along the thyroglossal tract). The home birth is not a cause. It explains only why a screen-detected, asymptomatic diagnosis instead presented at one month, as maternal T4 washed out.

Defining criteria Primary congenital hypothyroidism — elevated TSH with low T4 (in-context: "increased TSH and decreased T4"); the diagnosis is made by newborn screening, not by symptoms · Prolonged (pathologic) neonatal jaundice — unconjugated jaundice persisting beyond age 2 weeks; it is the finding that converts a sleepy feeder into a thyroid workup
Pertinent positives & negatives TSH 110 with T4 0.6 — primary (glandular) failure; excludes panhypopituitarism and any central cause · Macroglossia + hoarse cry — mucopolysaccharide deposition in tongue and larynx; the specific soft-tissue signature of thyroid hormone deficiency, not of sepsis or a storage disease at this age · Direct bilirubin 0.7 of 8 — unconjugated; excludes biliary atresia and the cholestatic causes of the sick jaundiced neonate, and points at slowed gut motility plus reduced hepatic conjugating enzyme activity · No goiter described — argues against dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency, both of which enlarge the gland under TSH drive · Mother ate well and took prenatal vitamins; infant is formula-fed — iodine deficiency is excluded (formula is iodine-supplemented) · Normal tone with decreased activity — hypometabolism, not a neuromuscular disease; hypotonia may appear later and its absence does not exclude the diagnosis · Symptomatic at 1 month, not at birth — maternal T4 crossed the placenta and masked the deficit; this timing is characteristic of the disease
Congenital hypothyroidism: locating the defect
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tellExcluded here by
Thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis/hypoplasia/ectopy)Failed formation or descent of the thyroid diverticulum from the pharyngeal floor along the thyroglossal duct; sporadic, no family historyHigh TSH, low T4, NO goiter, unremarkable maternal history; ectopic lingual tissue on scintigraphy(the answer)
Dyshormonogenesis (e.g., thyroid peroxidase defect)Autosomal recessive enzyme block in organification; gland present but cannot make hormone, so TSH drive enlarges itGoiter in a hypothyroid newborn; consanguinity or affected sibling; deafness if PendredNo goiter, no family history; a minority of cases
Iodine deficiencyMaternal dietary lack in an endemic region; substrate, not machinery, is missing; goitrousMaternal diet/geography stated; goiter in mother and infantBalanced diet + prenatal vitamins; all formula contains iodine
Central (panhypopituitarism)Pituitary/hypothalamic failure; TSH is the deficient hormoneLOW or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4; midline defects (cleft lip/palate), micropenis, hypoglycemiaTSH 110: the axis is intact and driving
Transplacental TSH-receptor stimulating antibodyMaternal Graves immunoglobulin G (IgG) crosses to the fetus → neonatal Graves, usually transient as antibody clears, generally within 6 monthsLow TSH, high T4, tachycardia, irritability, hyperphagia with poor weight gainDirection is inverted: TSH 110, T4 0.6, poor feeding and lethargy
Management, in one line A maternal blocking antibody against the TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) receptor is the rare counterpart of the stimulating antibody. It causes transient primary hypothyroidism with high TSH; scintigraphy can show no uptake, so ultrasound is needed to show the gland is present.
Decision spine Is TSH high or low? — High → primary; the pituitary causes are excluded · Is T4 low? — Yes → hypothyroid, not a compensated or antibody-stimulated state · Is there a goiter? — No → not dyshormonogenesis, not iodine deficiency · Is there a maternal story? — Diet fine, no Graves → no acquired/transplacental cause · What's left is the default — dysgenesis, the most common cause; the home birth explains the delay in detection, not the disease
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Newborn screen (heel prick at 24 to 48 hours)ScreenHigh TSH (some programs measure T4 first)Recall the infant for serum tests the same day
Serum TSH and free T4ConfirmsHigh TSH, low free T4; or low or normal TSH with low free T4Primary: start levothyroxine now. Central: check adrenal function and replace cortisol before levothyroxine unless adrenal function is intact, then pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Thyroid ultrasound or radionuclide scanCause, optionalEctopic gland, or no gland on ultrasound; or an enlarged gland in placeDysgenesis; or dyshormonogenesis. Never delays treatment

Scenario bank
  1. 3 wk M, home birth with no newborn screen, sleepy and feeding poorly, jaundiced since week 1, large tongue; TSH 140, T4 0.5 → Start levothyroxine now → Congenital hypothyroidism from thyroid dysgenesis
  2. 2 wk F with lethargy and poor feeding, firm anterior neck mass, older brother on levothyroxine, consanguineous parents; TSH 120, T4 0.4 → Dyshormonogenesis from a thyroid peroxidase defect → Levothyroxine; ultrasound shows an enlarged gland in place
  3. 5 d M with cleft palate, micropenis and fasting hypoglycemia; T4 low with TSH 0.8 → Central hypothyroidism from panhypopituitarism → Cortisol replacement before levothyroxine, then pituitary MRI
  4. 6 d F whose mother had Graves disease treated by thyroidectomy; infant tachycardic, irritable, poor weight gain despite hyperphagia; TSH undetectable, T4 elevated → Start a beta blocker and methimazole → Neonatal Graves disease from transplacental TSH receptor stimulating antibody
  5. Newborn screen at 48 hours returns TSH 60 with low T4; the infant is asymptomatic and feeding well on examination → Start levothyroxine without waiting for imaging → Congenital hypothyroidism
  6. 3 wk M with poor feeding and prolonged jaundice, TSH 90 and T4 0.6, no palpable goiter → Thyroid ultrasound or radionuclide uptake scan → An ectopic gland, or no gland on ultrasound, confirms dysgenesis
  7. 4 wk F starting levothyroxine for congenital hypothyroidism; the parent asks how to administer the crushed tablet → Mixing the dose into soy formula or an iron containing supplement → Crush and give in a small volume of water or breast milk
  8. 5 wk M with congenital hypothyroidism, total bilirubin 9 with direct 0.6, stools normally pigmented → Slowed gastrointestinal motility with reduced hepatic bilirubin conjugating enzyme activity → Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that resolves with levothyroxine
  9. 2 mo M diagnosed at 6 weeks and on levothyroxine for 4 weeks; TSH 45 with low normal free T4, parents confirm daily dosing → Increase the levothyroxine dose and recheck in 4 weeks → Under replacement
  10. 3 mo F born where newborn screening is unavailable, never treated, now with developmental delay, poor linear growth and constipation; TSH 180, T4 0.3 → Start levothyroxine immediately → Untreated congenital hypothyroidism
Decoy note The home birth is not a cause. It explains the missed newborn screen and therefore the unusual symptomatic presentation. The balanced maternal diet with prenatal vitamins excludes iodine deficiency. Primigravida, age 24, unremarkable family history: none of these points to a cause, although the absent family history modestly argues against a recessive enzyme defect.
Pearls High TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), low T4 (thyroxine) and no goiter mean dysgenesis; a goiter means a synthesis defect, and a low TSH means the pituitary. · Symptom onset at weeks to months, not at birth, is characteristic of congenital hypothyroidism. Placental maternal T4 covers the first weeks, so a normal newborn exam never reassures. · Unconjugated jaundice past 2 weeks of age calls for considering thyroid disease and galactosemia; conjugated jaundice at any age calls for considering a biliary cause. · Macroglossia plus hoarse cry is mucopolysaccharide deposition in hypothyroid soft tissue. It is distinct from Beckwith-Wiedemann (macroglossia with hemihyperplasia and hypoglycemia). · Treat on the screening result. Imaging to name the cause never delays levothyroxine, because the neurodevelopmental window is measured in weeks. Most children treated early and adequately have normal neurodevelopmental outcomes. · A goiter in a hypothyroid newborn points to a synthesis problem or an iodine problem; dysgenesis has no gland to enlarge. · In central hypothyroidism, give cortisol before levothyroxine unless adrenal function is shown to be intact: thyroid hormone is thought to accelerate cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Pairs with Jaundice in a Newborn shares the complaint of a jaundiced newborn with an abnormal screen. Ask: is the hyperbilirubinemia conjugated, and is the infant ill or merely slow? Thyroid Disease in an Adult covers the adult version of the same TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) direction logic. It also covers the dosing loop that this brief only points at. Part I Hypotonia in an Infant covers the other causes of low tone in infancy and the yearly TSH in Down syndrome.
Transferable rule In any hormone deficiency, the trophic hormone's direction locates the lesion. High TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) puts it in the gland; low TSH puts it in the pituitary. Within the gland, the presence or absence of an organ (goiter or none) separates a machinery defect from a formation defect.
Class-vs-memberDefective thyroid peroxidase activity: A minority of cases, and it almost always produces a goiter, which this exam does not describe; no family history in a recessive condition
True-fact-wrong-slotTransplacental TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) receptor–stimulating antibody: It causes neonatal Graves, with suppressed TSH, high T4 (thyroxine), tachycardia and hyperphagia. Every value and symptom here is inverted
Salient decoyIodine deficiency, endemic goiter: The balanced diet plus prenatal vitamins excludes it, and all formula contains iodine
Test-overrides-findingsPanhypopituitarism: TSH 110 proves the pituitary is working; central disease gives a low or inappropriately normal TSH plus midline defects and micropenis

Seizure with Fever in a Child

benign only inside the age window · intracranial signs · fontanelle and tone, not the neck · when to tapIs the child inside the febrile-seizure age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?

Source vignette Pt — 10 wk F, fever and vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsy an hour later, open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck, decreased tone · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned lumbar puncture, neuroimaging and reassurance with discharge
The decision point

At 10 weeks old, febrile seizure is excluded by age. Simple febrile seizures are defined between 6 months and 5 years. A child outside that window with fever and a seizure needs a meningitis workup by definition, before any other finding is weighed. Three other findings independently indicate the same step. A full anterior fontanelle and vomiting are signs of raised intracranial pressure. The drowsiness persisting an hour is a postictal period far beyond the ten minutes a simple febrile seizure allows. A supple neck is not reassuring, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants; read the fontanelle and the tone instead. Perform a lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Simple febrile seizure — age 6 months to 5 years, generalized, lasting under 15 minutes, with a brief postictal period under 10 minutes and rapid return to baseline, in a child with no signs of intracranial infection; the diagnosis is clinical and needs no laboratory studies or imaging · Findings that mandate urgent lumbar puncture — age outside 6 months to 5 years, signs of intracranial infection such as headache, vomiting, a bulging or full fontanelle or nuchal rigidity, prolonged altered mental status meaning a postictal period beyond 10 minutes, and a petechial rash concerning for meningococcal disease · Additional considerations for tapping — current antibiotic therapy, which masks meningitis, and an incomplete immunization history · The open-fontanelle exemption — signs of raised intracranial pressure usually require imaging before lumbar puncture, but an open fontanelle acts as a pop-off valve, limiting herniation risk and generally negating the need for a head computed tomography (CT) first
Pertinent positives & negatives Age 10 weeks — outside the febrile-seizure window entirely; this alone rules out discharge · Full anterior fontanelle — a sign of intracranial infection and raised pressure, and an indication to tap rather than a reason to image · Fontanelle open — acts as a pop-off valve, so CT is not needed first · Drowsy one hour after a 4-minute seizure — a postictal period beyond 10 minutes. This is prolonged altered mental status and an indication on its own · Weak suck and decreased tone — altered mental status in an infant, whose neurologic examination is feeding and tone rather than orientation · Neck supple — excludes nothing, because meningeal signs can be subtle or absent under 12 months · Seizure generalized, single, 4 minutes, now stopped — no benzodiazepine, since she is not seizing and it was under 5 minutes. No EEG (electroencephalography), since it was not focal, prolonged or recurrent · Skin normal — no petechiae, so meningococcemia is not the presentation; four other findings already indicate the tap · Vaccinations up to date — the incomplete-immunization consideration no longer applies, but the indication for the tap remains
Seizure with fever in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tellExcluded here by
Bacterial meningitis Can't missAny age, and infants localize poorly, so systemic and pressure signs substitute for neck signsSeizure with fever plus a full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia or prolonged altered mental status, with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture decidingNone (the answer to pursue)
Simple febrile seizureViral fever triggers a generalized seizure in a neurologically normal childAge 6 months to 5 years, under 15 minutes, back to baseline within 10 minutes, otherwise normal examinationAge 10 weeks, postictal drowsiness at 1 hour, full fontanelle
Complex febrile seizureThe same trigger, but focal, prolonged, or recurrent within 24 hoursFocal features, longer than 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours; EEG may be considered, and imaging only with abnormal or focal examination findingsThe seizure was single, generalized and 4 minutes
Herpes simplex encephalitis Can't missNeonatal or later, and parenchymal rather than meningealProlonged altered mental status with focal or temporal findings and CSF lymphocytes; red cells may be presentNot excluded; the same tap tests for it, and acyclovir is given until it is excluded
Meningococcemia Can't missN. meningitidis sepsis with rapid decompensationPetechial or purpuric rash with fever and shock, where antibiotics precede the tapSkin examination normal, normotensive
Abusive head trauma Can't missInfant with subdural collectionsSeizure with a bulging fontanelle and retinal hemorrhages, with increased irritabilityNot excluded by the stated findings
Decision spine How old? — Ten weeks → outside the window, so this is not a febrile seizure and discharge is ruled out · Is she seizing now? — No, it stopped in 4 minutes → no benzodiazepine · Was it focal, prolonged or recurrent? — No → no EEG (electroencephalography) · Any sign of intracranial infection? — Full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia, still drowsy → yes · Does she need a CT first? — The fontanelle is open → no, so perform the lumbar puncture
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to

Lumbar punctureBy branchCSF pleocytosis; lymphocytes, and red cells may be present, in herpes simplex encephalitisMeningitis or encephalitis; tap for age under 6 months, full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness
Serum electrolytes and glucoseBy branchLow sodium or glucoseProvoked seizure; order with vomiting or diarrhea
Head CT or magnetic resonance imagingBy branchSubdural blood, a mass or edemaFocal signs, or papilledema with a closed fontanelle; infant with retinal hemorrhages
EEGBy branchFocal or epileptiform dischargesMay be considered for a complex febrile seizure, meaning one that is focal, over 15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours

Scenario bank
  1. 10-week-old girl with fever, vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsiness persisting an hour later, an open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck and decreased tone → Lumbar puncture → Age outside the window plus signs of intracranial infection
  2. 18-month-old boy with temperature 39.1 C and a single 3-minute generalized seizure who is alert with a normal examination 20 minutes later → Reassurance and discharge → Simple febrile seizure
  3. 2-year-old girl with fever who is still convulsing 8 minutes after the seizure began → Intravenous lorazepam → Duration gates the benzodiazepine
  4. 3-year-old boy with fever, a generalized seizure, a spreading petechial rash and hypotension → Give empiric intravenous antibiotics immediately and perform the lumbar puncture afterward → Meningococcemia
  5. 12-month-old girl with fever and a seizure who has papilledema and a new focal neurologic deficit, with a closed anterior fontanelle → Antibiotics, then head CT, then lumbar puncture → The imaging exception
  6. 6-week-old boy, afebrile, with a seizure, a bulging fontanelle and retinal hemorrhages on fundoscopy → Neuroimaging → Abusive head trauma
  7. 4-year-old boy, now postictal after his third seizure of this febrile illness, this one left-sided and lasting 20 minutes → Electroencephalography → Complex febrile seizure (focal, 20 minutes, recurrent); EEG may be considered when a febrile seizure is focal or recurrent; he is no longer seizing, so no lorazepam, and a complex seizure warrants more than reassurance
  8. 2-year-old with fever, seizure and persistently altered mental status whose cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with red blood cells → Herpes simplex encephalitis → Add acyclovir to empiric therapy
  9. Why an open anterior fontanelle removes the usual requirement for head CT before lumbar puncture → It acts as a pop-off valve that decompresses rising intracranial pressure, limiting herniation risk → The anatomy suspends the rule
  10. Infant with fever, petechiae and hypotension in whom the lumbar puncture will be delayed; which action is inappropriate → Delaying antibiotics until the lumbar puncture is completed → Treat first, tap after
  11. 2 yo M, 2 days of rhinorrhea, fever 39.2 C this morning, a 3-minute generalized seizure, sleepy and confused when paramedics arrived, now alert and playful with a normal examination; uncle has epilepsy; immunizations current → Reassurance and discharge home → simple febrile seizure; the postictal drowsiness has resolved and an uncle's epilepsy changes nothing
  12. Parents of a 2 yo after a first simple febrile seizure ask what to expect → About 30% have another; epilepsy risk stays about 1 to 2% → antipyretics do not prevent the next one
  13. 2 yo back to baseline after a brief generalized febrile seizure, but with 2 days of profuse vomiting and diarrhea and dry mucous membranes → Serum electrolytes and glucose → hypoglycemia or hyponatremia can provoke a seizure
  14. 11-month-old boy is evaluated after a 2-minute generalized seizure at home. Temperature 39.2 °C, heart rate 150/min. He is now alert and playful with a normal examination. He has received no pneumococcal or Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine doses → Lumbar puncture → incomplete immunization at 6 to 12 months lowers the bar to tap; maintenance antiseizure drugs are usually not indicated; EEG is not recommended after a simple febrile seizure with a normal examination
Decoy note A supple neck excludes nothing, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants. The criteria list substitutes the fontanelle, the tone and the feeding. The rest of the examination is normal: tympanic membranes, oropharynx, lungs, abdomen and skin. With no source found, this strengthens the case for tapping rather than weakening it. When every peripheral source is excluded in a febrile infant with neurologic signs, the meninges are what is left. Up-to-date vaccinations remove one of the modifiers on the list but leave the four indications already present.
Counseling, and what each test is for Recurrence — about 30% have another febrile seizure · Epilepsy — risk slightly raised, about 1 to 2% · Antipyretics — treat discomfort, do not prevent the next seizure · Course — resolves by school age, with no effect on development · Risk factors — fever of 39.5 °C or higher, a viral illness such as roseola or influenza, recent immunization, a family history of febrile seizures or epilepsy · Timing — usually the first day of the illness, sometimes before the viral symptoms appear · Brain imaging — focal neurologic signs · EEG — recurrent unprovoked seizures, not a simple febrile seizure · Admission — not back to neurologic baseline · Electrolytes and glucose — vomiting or diarrhea, since hypoglycemia and hyponatremia can provoke a seizure · Lumbar puncture — also at 6 to 12 months with incomplete pneumococcal or Hib immunization, or when already on antibiotics
Pearls Fever with seizure under 6 months, or with a full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness, needs a lumbar puncture. An open fontanelle needs no CT. · The febrile-seizure diagnosis has an age gate on both ends, 6 months and 5 years. It is the fastest disqualifier, so check it before anything else. · An open fontanelle is a pop-off valve, so infants tolerate rising intracranial pressure that would herniate an older child. The CT-before-tap rule therefore generally does not apply to them. · The same finding can be both the indication and the apparent contraindication. Then ask what the rule is protecting against, and whether that risk exists in this patient. · Infants may lack neck signs; read the fontanelle, the tone, the suck and the cry instead. A supple neck excludes nothing under 12 months. · A postictal period beyond 10 minutes is altered mental status, not a long febrile seizure, and it indicates a tap on its own. · With petechiae and hypotension, reverse the order: antibiotics first, tap after. A sterilized Gram stain is an acceptable price.
Pairs with Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn covers the workup when there is no seizure, up to the decision to tap. This brief covers what a seizure adds to that decision. Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the cerebrospinal fluid grid that interprets the fluid once it is obtained. Ask: is this child inside the age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?
Transferable rule For a benign diagnosis defined by an age range, check the age before weighing the findings, because age disqualifies it first. When a rule and a finding point in opposite directions, ask what the rule was built to prevent. If the anatomy has already prevented it, the rule does not apply.
True-fact-wrong-slotNeuroimaging: The rule exists to prevent herniation, and an open fontanelle decompresses the pressure, so the risk it guards against is not present and CT is generally unnecessary
Mirror twinReassurance and discharge: Requires age 6 months to 5 years; at 10 weeks this was never a febrile seizure, and the postictal drowsiness and full fontanelle each independently disqualify it
Salient decoyElectroencephalography: EEG may be considered for seizures that are prolonged, recurrent or focal, and this was single, generalized and four minutes
True-fact-wrong-slotIntravenous lorazepam: Given for generalized convulsions lasting over 5 minutes, and she stopped at four and is no longer seizing

Cyanosis in the Newborn

lung, heart or airway before a lesion · work of breathing, oxygen response, two limbs · normal exam: the trigger decidesIs he working to breathe, does oxygen help, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing?

Source vignette Pt — 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen · Imaging — ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned respiratory distress syndrome, d-transposition of the great arteries and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
The decision point

Three bedside findings settle the sort before any lesion is considered. He is working to breathe (grunting, flaring and retracting); cyanotic heart disease produces comfortable tachypnea, not distress. His saturation rises from 65% to 92% on oxygen. That cannot happen in d-transposition, where systemic flow bypasses the lungs entirely. The two limbs read the same, so nothing is shunting right-to-left across the duct. That leaves parenchymal disease. A 32-week infant with ground-glass opacification and air bronchograms has surfactant deficiency: respiratory distress syndrome.

Sometimes the examination is instead a list of normals: no murmur, symmetric pulses, equal four-extremity pressures, clear lungs, no retractions, no stridor. These normals already exclude lung and heart. The remaining finding is temporal. Ask: What brings the cyanosis on, and what relieves it? Cyanosis on latching that clears with crying is nasal obstruction, because neonates are obligate nasal breathers and crying opens the oral airway. The inverse pattern, cyanosis worsened by crying, is a tet spell.

Defining criteria Oxygen responsiveness — saturation rises substantially with supplemental oxygen in alveolar disease; it does not in d-transposition, because most systemic flow bypasses the pulmonary vasculature · Preductal vs. postductal — the right upper extremity is preductal and the lower extremities postductal; a higher preductal saturation means right-to-left ductal shunting · Ductal closure clock — the ductus arteriosus begins to constrict as early as 12 hours after birth, so ductal-dependent lesions declare after that, not at minutes · RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) risk — inversely related to gestational age, highest at ≤28 weeks; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce but do not eliminate it · Bilateral choanal atresia — incomplete canalization of the posterior nasal passage; cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying, with noisy breathing (stertor), symptomatic shortly after birth · Why crying relieves it — neonates are obligate nasal breathers; hypoxia and hypercapnia trigger crying, which opens the oral airway and temporarily bypasses the obstruction · The bedside test — inability to pass a catheter through the nares into the oropharynx, confirmed by CT (computed tomography) or nasal endoscopy · The stability gate — a cyanotic newborn whose hypoxemia does not correct on oxygen gets echocardiography, and prostaglandin E1 is added when the infant is hemodynamically unstable, because instability is what raises concern for a ductal-dependent lesion
Pertinent positives & negatives Grunting, flaring, retractions — work of breathing; this is lung disease, and it excludes the two structural cardiac options, which give tachypnea without distress · 65% → 92% on oxygen — the alveoli can be recruited; excludes d-transposition outright · Right upper and left lower extremity both 65% — no ductal gradient; argues against persistent pulmonary hypertension and against a coarctation presentation · Cyanosis at minutes of life — too early for ductal closure, which begins at about 12 hours; coarctation cannot yet have declared · 32 weeks, 1.7 kg — the base rate for surfactant deficiency; RDS incidence rises as gestational age falls · Ground-glass with air bronchograms and low lung volumes — RDS; transient tachypnea gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures, and pulmonary hypertension a clear or oligemic film · Grade 1/6 systolic murmur — soft and non-specific, consistent with a physiologically open duct rather than a structural lesion · A dose of antenatal glucocorticoids — lowers the risk but never excludes the diagnosis · PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) — raises concern for group B streptococcal pneumonia even after intrapartum penicillin; that pneumonia is clinically very hard to tell from RDS · Acrocyanosis — peripheral cyanosis of hands, feet, and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes is a normal finding in the first 24–48 hours of life; central cyanosis (mucous membranes blue) requires workup
Cyanosis in the newborn: sorting by physiology
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) tellExcluded here by
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency; alveolar collapse minutes to hours after birthDistress plus oxygen responsiveness plus ground-glass with air bronchograms in a preterm infant(the answer)
Transient tachypnea of the newbornRetained fetal lung fluid; term or late pretermMild distress and cyanosis; perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissuresSevere distress; the film is ground-glass, not streaky
Persistent pulmonary hypertension Can't missHigh pulmonary vascular resistance; right-to-left ductal shuntPreductal saturation above postductal; film often normal, poorly oxygen-responsiveEqual limb saturations; oxygen worked; the film is abnormal
d-Transposition of the great arteriesParallel circulations; deoxygenated blood to the bodyCyanosis without retractions, and oxygen does not helpGrunting and retractions; 65% to 92% on oxygen
Coarctation of the aortaDuctal-dependent systemic flow; shock when the duct shutsPostductal saturation below preductal, presenting after ~12 hoursEqual limb saturations at 30 minutes of life
Cyanosis with a normal examination: sorting by trigger
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Bilateral choanal atresiaPosterior nasal passage fails to canalize; the obligate nasal breather obstructs whenever his mouth closesWorse with feeding, better with crying; stertor; catheter will not pass(the answer)
Tetralogy of FallotRight ventricular outflow obstruction; a spell when systemic resistance fallsCyanosis worse with crying and agitation (the inverted trigger) plus a murmurCrying makes him pink; there is no murmur
Transposition of the great arteriesParallel circulations; deoxygenated blood to the bodyConstant cyanosis unchanged by feeding or crying, unimproved by oxygenThe cyanosis comes and goes with what he is doing
Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresiaAspiration through a fistula or from a blind pouchCoughing and choking with feeds, respiratory distress, a tube that coilsHe fed well without coughing; lungs are clear
LaryngomalaciaSupraglottic collapse on inspirationInspiratory stridor worse supine and with exertion; cyanosis uncommonNo stridor at all
Transient tachypnea of the newbornRetained fetal lung fluid after deliveryTachypnea with flaring, retractions and grunting in the first hoursNo respiratory distress of any kind
MethemoglobinemiaOxidized hemoglobin iron cannot carry oxygenPersistent cyanosis that does not improve with crying or with oxygenHis cyanosis clears every time he cries
Neonatal sepsisBacterial infection with varied, nonspecific signsTemperature instability, lethargy, poor feedingNormal temperature; vigorous; blue only at the breast
Intraventricular hemorrhageGerminal matrix bleed, mainly in preterm infantsLethargy, hypotonia, apnea, seizures; found on head ultrasoundTerm infant with a normal neurologic picture
Management, in one line Support RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) with CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure). Reserve mechanical ventilation and exogenous surfactant for severe or failing cases. In the heart branch, management is instead a prostaglandin infusion to hold the duct open; in the pulmonary-hypertension branch, it is oxygen and inhaled nitric oxide. For the nasal obstruction, the first step is an oral airway with orogastric feeding to bypass the obstruction, and definitive treatment is surgical repair.
Decision spine Is he working to breathe? — Grunting, flaring, retracting → lung, not heart · Does oxygen help? — 65% to 92% → not a fixed right-to-left shunt, so not transposition · Do the limbs differ? — No → nothing is shunting across the duct · How old is he? — Thirty minutes → the duct is still open; ductal-dependent lesions have not declared · What does the film show? — Ground-glass with air bronchograms in a 32-weeker → surfactant deficiency · If every examination finding is normal — sort by the trigger: worse with feeding and better with crying is nasal obstruction; worse with crying is a tet spell; unchanged by either is a fixed shunt.
FigureApproach to neonatal cyanosisshow

Redrawn rather than reproduced. The one deliberate change from the usual published version: echocardiography and prostaglandin are shown as separate steps with the stability gate between them, because bundling them is what makes the sequencing question hard.

Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Pulse oximetry, right hand and a footFirstPreductal higher than postductalRight-to-left ductal shunt: PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn), or coarctation after about 12 hours
Trial of 100% oxygenNextSaturation rises substantiallyLung disease; no rise means a fixed shunt such as transposition
Chest radiographNextGround-glass with air bronchograms and low volumesRDS in a preterm; streaking with fissure fluid is transient tachypnea of the newborn
Catheter through each narisBy branchCatheter will not passChoanal atresia when cyanosis worsens with feeding and clears with crying
CT or nasal endoscopyConfirmsPosterior nasal obstructionChoanal atresia; look for the rest of CHARGE
EchocardiographyConfirmsStructural lesion or high pulmonary pressuresHypoxemia that oxygen does not correct; prostaglandin E1 added only if unstable
Any testing for acrocyanosisSkipPink mucous membranesNormal in the first 24 to 48 hours: reassurance
Echocardiogram, methemoglobin level, blood cultures or head ultrasound for cyanosis only with feedsSkipNormal oximetry, pulses, heart exam and film; pink when cryingPass the catheter first; nothing in the exam points to the heart, the blood, infection or the brain
Scenario bank
  1. 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen, ground-glass with air bronchograms → Respiratory distress syndrome → Surfactant deficiency
  2. 32 wk with respiratory distress syndrome at 30 minutes of life, breathing spontaneously → Start CPAP → Surfactant and intubation are reserved for severe disease
  3. 32 wk on CPAP with a rising oxygen requirement and worsening retractions at 6 hours → Intubate and give exogenous surfactant → CPAP has failed
  4. Term newborn at 14 hours, cyanosis with comfortable tachypnea and no retractions, clear lungs, a loud single S2, equal pulses, saturation unchanged on 100% oxygen → Obtain echocardiography → an anatomic right-to-left shunt; prostaglandin is added only if the infant is unstable
  5. Term after meconium-stained fluid, distress, right hand 95% and foot 78%, film clear with decreased vascularity → Inhaled nitric oxide → Persistent pulmonary hypertension
  6. Why an infant with respiratory distress syndrome grunts → To generate end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli open → Flaring lowers airway resistance
  7. 2-hour-old, cyanotic when latched at the breast, pink when crying, no murmur, clear lungs, normal four-extremity pressures → Bilateral choanal atresia → Obligate nasal breathing
  8. Newborn with cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying → Pass a catheter through each naris→ CT or nasal endoscopy confirms it
  9. 6-month-old with tetralogy of Fallot, sudden deep cyanosis and inconsolable crying → Knee-to-chest positioning with supplemental oxygen → A tet spell, triggered by crying
  10. Why crying temporarily relieves the cyanosis of bilateral choanal atresia → Crying bypasses the obstructed nose→ by opening the oral airway; Neonates are obligate nasal breathers
  11. Term newborn with cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen and a single S2, now with weak pulses, poor perfusion and a falling blood pressure → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → instability licenses the drug before the picture
  12. Why supplemental oxygen fails to raise the saturation in transposition of the great arteries → Parallel circulations bypass the lungs→ systemic blood bypasses the lungs entirely; a fixed anatomic right-to-left shunt
  13. Term newborn cyanotic from the first hours with a loud single S2 and no murmur, unimproved on oxygen → Transposition of the great arteries → mixing flow is too low-velocity to make a murmur
  14. 1-day-old boy born at 39 weeks, feeding well. Heart rate 138/min, respiratory rate 42/min, afebrile. No murmur; femoral pulses 2+. Pulse oximetry: right hand 97%, right foot 93%. One hour later: right hand 97%, right foot 93%. → Echocardiography → a foot reading under 95% with a gap over 3% on two measures an hour apart fails the screen; with no other cause of hypoxemia found, echocardiography follows, and a second retest is not part of the algorithm
  15. Newborn at 5 minutes of life, heart rate 120/min, respiratory rate 50/min, vigorous cry, flexing extremities, cyanosis of hands feet and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes → Reassurance and routine care → acrocyanosis
  16. 6-day-old breastfed M, unconjugated bilirubin 14, weight 11% below birth weight, 3 wet diapers on day 5, nursing every 4 hours, mother milk just came in → Breastfeed every 2 to 3 hours and follow up in 1 day → lactation failure jaundice
  17. 10-day-old breastfed F, unconjugated bilirubin 16, weight appropriate, 8 wet diapers daily, nursing well every 2 to 3 hours → Breast milk jaundice → continue breastfeeding and monitor
  18. 1-day-old term boy whose face turns blue within a minute of every feed and pinks up when he cries; normal heart and lung exam, pulse oximetry 97% in the right hand and 96% in the foot; a catheter cannot be passed through either naris beyond the nasopharynx → Oral airway and orogastric feeding → Bilateral choanal atresia; confirm with CT or nasal endoscopy, then surgical repair
Decoy note Antenatal glucocorticoids are genuinely protective, but they only lower the risk of RDS (respiratory distress syndrome); they do not treat it away. A grade 1/6 murmur is soft and non-specific. In a 30-minute-old it is almost certainly a physiologically open duct rather than a lesion. PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) raises concern for group B streptococcal pneumonia even after intrapartum penicillin; that pneumonia is clinically very hard to tell from RDS, so antibiotics are started empirically pending cultures. In the normal-examination case, six normal findings each exclude one diagnosis, and the only positive finding is the timing. A primigravida with an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, and an infant who voided and passed meconium, are inert findings. They only establish that the baby is well, which is the precondition for the sort.
Pearls Grunting with retractions that improves on oxygen is lung disease; in a preterm infant with ground-glass and air bronchograms that is surfactant deficiency. · Work of breathing is the first sort: grunting, flaring and retractions mean lung; comfortable tachypnea with cyanosis means heart. · Oxygen is diagnostic and therapeutic: it separates alveolar disease from a fixed shunt and treats RDS (respiratory distress syndrome). It is occasionally harmful: in hypoplastic left heart syndrome it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and shifts right ventricular output to the lungs. · A lesion that depends on the duct presents when the duct closes, from about 12 hours onward. Cyanosis in the delivery room is lung disease, failed transition or transposition. · Antenatal glucocorticoids stimulate fetal surfactant synthesis and lower the risk of RDS; a dosed 32-week infant can still have it. · Hypoxia in RDS is self-amplifying. Collapse causes hypoxia, hypoxia constricts the pulmonary vasculature, and the resulting right-to-left shunt deepens the cyanosis. Shunt physiology can therefore be present without a shunt lesion. · Newborns are obligate nasal breathers. Nasal obstruction therefore gives cyanosis that worsens when the mouth is occluded by feeding and improves when it opens with crying. · The inverse pattern is the tet spell: cyanosis worsens with crying and agitation and is relieved by knee-to-chest positioning. · Pass a catheter through each naris first. It is a free bedside test, and imaging only confirms what the catheter suggested. · Choanal atresia may belong to CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, atresia choanae, retardation of growth, genital and ear abnormalities). Unilateral disease often goes unrecognized until childhood, when it presents as chronic unilateral nasal discharge. · Tachypnea without distress points to the heart: fast breathing with no flaring, grunting or retractions, and clear lungs. Work of breathing points to the lung. · A loud single S2 with no murmur is characteristic of transposition. The absent murmur is a positive finding rather than a missing one, because flow through the mixing shunts is too low-velocity to generate sound.
Pairs with Part II Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers the film-based sort among the parenchymal causes. Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers the lesion catalog once the sort points to the heart. Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers the newborn clock (which diagnosis belongs at which hour) and includes choanal atresia in its minutes-to-hours group. Ask: is he working to breathe, does oxygen help, do the limbs differ, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing? Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the step after a positive catheter test: which syndrome includes the choanal atresia. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers acrocyanosis as the decoy beside a trisomy 18 murmur; ask: are the lips and tongue pink?
Transferable rule When a finding has both a lung and a heart cause, sort by physiology before naming a disease. The bedside triad of work of breathing, oxygen response and a pre-to-postductal difference decides which group of diagnoses to consider. When the sort finds nothing abnormal, the pattern in time is the key finding. A trigger that runs the opposite way excludes the lesion it resembles.
Unchecked attributeContinuous positive airway pressure: a respiratory rate of 66 reads as distress, but the stem negates flaring, grunting and retractions and reports clear lungs. The rate was checked and the work of breathing was not.
Salient decoyd-Transposition of the great arteries: Transposition gives cyanosis without grunting or retractions, and oxygen does not improve it; the stem shows both the retractions and a rise to 92%
True-fact-wrong-slotPersistent pulmonary hypertension: That is a consequence of the atelectasis, not the primary disease; PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn) gives a preductal-postductal gradient and a clear film, and neither is present
Mirror twinTransient tachypnea of the newborn: it is mild and gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures; this infant has severe distress and a ground-glass film
Unchecked attributeCoarctation of the aorta: The duct does not begin to constrict until about 12 hours; at 30 minutes it is open, and coarctation would show a lower postductal saturation, not equal ones
True-fact-wrong-slotTetralogy of Fallot: its trigger is inverted. Tet spells come with crying and agitation, which is what turns this baby pink, and a murmur would be expected
Class-vs-memberTracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia: Aspiration through a fistula brings coughing, choking and respiratory distress; this infant latched, sucked well, and has clear lungs
Class-vs-memberLaryngomalacia: It obstructs at the larynx and announces itself with inspiratory stridor, which is explicitly absent; cyanosis is uncommon

Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment

who is screened early · T-score vs Z-score · when to treat · drug cautionsHas every risk factor been counted, and does each one point the way you assume?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Screen every woman at 65 with DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry). Run the risk-factor list before applying that default:

  • Exam shorthand (question banks): any one risk factor (prior fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, low body weight, chronic glucocorticoids) means DEXA now; the BHOF (Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation) 2022 guide likewise says to consider DEXA in younger postmenopausal women with a clinical risk factor. The task force rule differs (next line).
  • USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) 2025: postmenopausal and under 65 with a risk factor such as low body weight, parental hip fracture, smoking or excess alcohol (the USPSTF also lists menopausal status), use a clinical risk tool such as FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool), then DEXA if the risk is raised; no fixed threshold. Men: evidence insufficient (not a recommendation against). Androgen deprivation therapy: BHOF says to consider DEXA.

Obesity protects bone; low body weight (under 58 kg) is the risk factor. A hip or vertebral fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis without a scan.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria T-score – against a young adult peak; postmenopausal women and men 50 or older: -1.0 or above normal, -1.0 to -2.5 osteopenia, -2.5 or below osteoporosis · Z-score – against age- and sex-matched peers; premenopausal women, men under 50, children: -2.0 or below is below expected and needs a secondary-cause search · Clinical osteoporosis – a hip or vertebral fragility fracture, regardless of T-score
Risk factors Nonmodifiable – advanced age, postmenopausal (the entry condition for screening under 65, not a trigger by itself), low body weight, White or Asian, malabsorption, hypercortisolism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic liver or kidney disease · Modifiable – smoking, excess alcohol, inactivity, glucocorticoids, anticonvulsants, proton pump inhibitors, low vitamin D or calcium, estrogen deficiency (premature menopause, oophorectomy), aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation therapy · Family history – FRAX asks about a parental hip fracture
Management and treatment
Management ladder: osteoporosis
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Smoking cessation, calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention; always concurrent, never enough alone once a risk factor existsAge 65: DEXA. Risk factor: DEXA now (exam) or consider DEXA (BHOF) or risk tool first (USPSTF)
2Check calcium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D and creatinine; correct low vitamin D firstT-score -2.5 or below, hip or vertebral fragility fracture, or osteopenia with FRAX 20% major or 3% hip
3Bisphosphonate: upright with water, stay upright 30 minutes; drug holiday after about 5 years oral or 3 years intravenous if low riskVery high risk: an anabolic agent (teriparatide or abaloparatide)
Drug cautions Bisphosphonate – esophagitis; long-term osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fracture · Denosumab – rebound vertebral fractures if stopped abruptly; never simply discontinue · Romosozumab – cardiovascular boxed warning · Raloxifene – lowers breast cancer risk but raises venous thromboembolism · Height loss or kyphosis – vertebral imaging
Practice
  1. 55-year-old woman asks when to check her bones menopause at 50 body mass index 31 Never smoked; no fractures; no parental hip fracture BP (blood pressure) 126/80 mm Hg · no glucocorticoid use → DEXA at 65 → no trigger on either list; menopause at a normal age with no risk factor waits until 65 (the USPSTF lists menopausal status but wants a risk factor beyond it): DEXA at 65; obesity protects bone
  2. 56-year-old woman, postmenopausal, asks about bone screening weighs 52 kg smokes a pack a day; her mother fractured a hip No fractures of her own; no glucocorticoids BP 122/76 mm Hg · body mass index 19 → Run FRAX now → DEXA now (the exam shorthand) is not offered; of these, the USPSTF step is a clinical risk tool such as FRAX, then DEXA if risk is raised; no drug before a diagnosis
  3. 68-year-old woman has never had bone density testing feels well and walks daily no fractures, no falls Takes no medications; never smoked; asks whether she needs a scan BP 136/82 mm Hg · body mass index 24 → DEXA now → every woman 65 or older is screened with DEXA; a risk tool alone does not replace it
  4. 60-year-old woman has a DEXA T-score of -1.8 at the hip no fractures of her own her father fractured a hip at 78 Nonsmoker BP 128/80 mm Hg · calcium and vitamin D normal → Run FRAX → osteopenia: run FRAX and treat if the 10-year risk is 20% or more for a major fracture or 3% or more for a hip fracture
  5. 32-year-old woman has a fragility fracture of the wrist fell from standing height on a sidewalk regular periods; no glucocorticoids DEXA ordered to evaluate her bones BP 108/68 mm Hg · body mass index 18 · Z-score -2.3 → Z-score; secondary-cause workup → a premenopausal patient is read by the Z-score, and a score of -2.0 or below sends you after secondary causes: celiac disease, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, an eating disorder, amenorrhea (her regular periods argue against it)
  6. 48-year-old woman has taken prednisone 10 mg daily for 4 months for sarcoidosis expects to continue for a year Still menstruating; no fractures BP 132/84 mm Hg · body mass index 26 → DEXA now → the ACR (American College of Rheumatology) 2022 guideline recommends bone density testing soon after starting glucocorticoids in an adult taking 2.5 mg/day or more for over 3 months, with FRAX from age 40
  7. 57-year-old woman with a T-score of -2.7 is about to start alendronate rarely goes outdoors in winter drinks no milk No calcium or vitamin D level on file; no kidney disease BP 124/78 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Check vitamin D and calcium first → check calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D first: an untreated vitamin D deficiency turns a bisphosphonate into hypocalcemia
  8. 64-year-old man starts androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer no fractures, no falls no glucocorticoids Asks whether his bones need checking BP 138/84 mm Hg · body mass index 27 · testosterone castrate level → Screen with DEXA now → androgen deprivation therapy (and an aromatase inhibitor in a woman) is a specific cause of bone loss; BHOF says to consider DEXA for it, although USPSTF finds the evidence for screening men in general insufficient
  9. 57-year-old woman has back pain after bending to lift a laundry basket radiograph: vertebral compression fracture no trauma No DEXA on file BP 130/80 mm Hg · calcium, vitamin D and creatinine normal → Start a bisphosphonate now → a vertebral or hip fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis by itself: start a bisphosphonate now
  10. 57-year-old woman who smokes asks for hormone therapy to protect her bones T-score -2.6 no hot flashes or night sweats Smokes a pack a day BP 134/86 mm Hg · calcium, vitamin D and creatinine normal → Decline estrogen; start alendronate → avoid estrogen: smoking adds to its venous thromboembolism risk, and hormone therapy is not first-line for bone; raloxifene also raises venous thromboembolism risk and is not first-line; a bisphosphonate treats a T-score of -2.6
  11. 70-year-old woman on alendronate for 8 years has thigh pain aching for weeks, worse with walking no fall Radiograph: cortical thickening with a transverse line in the lateral femoral shaft Afebrile · calcium normal → Atypical femoral fracture → thigh pain after years of bisphosphonate is an atypical femoral fracture: image both femurs
Transferable rule

Run the risk-factor list first and apply the age default only when it comes back empty. Check that each variable points the way you assume: obesity raises cardiovascular, endometrial and sleep apnea risk but lowers osteoporosis risk.

Puberty

normal staging: sexual maturity rating (SMR) · early puberty: central or peripheral · virilization in a girlIs the stage right for the age, and if not, which hormones are on board, from where?

StagingEarly pubertyVirilizationPractice
Bottom line

Stage breast and hair separately; a stage wrong for the age needs a workup.

  • Precocious puberty: secondary sexual characteristics before 8 in girls or 9 in boys.
  • Delayed puberty: no breast development by 13, or no testicular enlargement by 14.
  • Central, GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) dependent: the whole axis turns on; consonant, progressive, LH (luteinizing hormone) pubertal.
  • Peripheral, GnRH-independent: sex hormone from gonad, adrenal or an exogenous source.
  • Virilization: clitoral enlargement in a girl; normal adrenarche never causes it.

Breast tissue means estrogen; an androgen-only source gives hair, acne and odor without breasts.

Staging and normal timing
Sexual maturity rating: the phrase that decides each stage
StageBreastPubic hair
1Papilla elevation onlyNone, or vellus only
2Bud: small mound under a widening areolaSparse, straight, lightly pigmented
3Beyond the areola, one contourDarker, coarser, curled; sparse over the pubis
4Areola and papilla form a second moundAdult quality across the pubis, sparing the medial thighs
5Areola recedes; papilla projects aloneAdult quantity, spreads to the medial thighs
Defining criteria One number – only when breast and hair agree · Discordant stages – a finding; hair well ahead of breast suggests an adrenal source · First sign – thelarche in girls; testes 4 mL or more in boys · Peak height velocity – SMR 2 to 3 in girls, SMR 4 in boys · Menarche – SMR 4, about 2 to 3 years after thelarche, about 6 months after peak velocity
Early puberty
McCune-Albright syndrome Triad – peripheral precocious puberty, irregular café-au-lait macules, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (recurrent fractures) · Mechanism – a somatic mosaic activating GNAS (the G protein alpha-s gene) mutation keeps a G protein switched on; any tissue carrying it secretes autonomously, so thyrotoxicosis, acromegaly or Cushing syndrome can accompany or replace the precocity · Family history – silent; postzygotic, not inherited; no added recurrence risk
Read a pigmented patch: number, border, distribution, color
SyndromeThe skin
McCune-AlbrightOften large and segmental; irregular; respecting the midline
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)Six or more, smooth, axillary freckling; precocity via optic glioma
Tuberous sclerosisHypopigmented ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch; seizures
Sturge-Weber; Peutz-JeghersRed-purple port-wine stain; 1 to 5 mm perioral macules; no precocity
Management Central – GnRH agonist, because the axis drives it · Peripheral – treat the source; a GnRH agonist does nothing · McCune-Albright – in girls, aromatase inhibitor or estrogen-receptor blockade
Virilization in a girl: which source?
The markers DHEAS – almost only from the adrenal zona reticularis; urine 17-ketosteroids rise with it · Testosterone – mostly ovarian in a girl · High DHEAS, normal testosterone, normal pelvic ultrasound – adrenal; far above range in a child is a tumor until proven otherwise; many pediatric virilizing adrenal tumors are carcinomas · High 17-hydroxyprogesterone – nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, the commoner adrenal cause
Practice
  1. 6-year-old girl is evaluated for breast budding and pubic hair two large hyperpigmented macules with irregular borders confined to the left chest and back, without freckling Long-bone fractures at ages 4 and 5 Afebrile · no headache, emesis or visual change → McCune-Albright syndrome → peripheral precocity, irregular segmental macules and recurrent fractures (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia) are the triad; only two macules, irregular borders and no freckling argue against neurofibromatosis type 1 (six or more smooth macules, usually with freckling), and breast budding excludes an androgen-only adrenal tumor
  2. 6-year-old girl has breast development and pubic hair height crossing percentiles upward bone age advanced to 9 years Skin entirely normal; no headache, emesis or visual change Afebrile · blood pressure (BP) 100/62 mm Hg → Measure basal LH with GnRH-stimulation testing if not diagnostic → consonant, progressive puberty with an advanced bone age suggests the axis is on, and normal skin argues against McCune-Albright: a pubertal basal LH confirms it, and a GnRH stimulation test settles a nondiagnostic level; waiting misses progressive puberty, and brain imaging follows confirmation
  3. 5-year-old girl was diagnosed with central precocious puberty this week LH rose after GnRH stimulation bone age advanced No headache, emesis or visual change; parents ask about next steps Afebrile · neurologic examination normal → Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain → younger onset raises the risk of a central nervous system lesion: image the brain for confirmed central puberty in a girl under 6 or a boy under 9, before treating or reassuring
  4. 2-year-old girl has breast budding noticed 3 months ago no pubic or axillary hair growth velocity normal Bone age matches her chronological age Afebrile · height and weight at the 50th percentile → Reassurance and observation → isolated breast development with normal growth velocity and a bone age matching age is premature thelarche: observe, without hormone testing or imaging
  5. 14-year-old boy is brought in because he is the shortest in his class no testicular enlargement height at the 3rd percentile His father entered puberty late Afebrile · examination otherwise normal → Obtain a bone age → no testicular enlargement by 14 is delayed puberty; the bone age comes before treatment or reassurance; delayed, with a late-blooming parent, it fits constitutional delay of growth and puberty
  6. 7-year-old girl has 6 months of pubic and axillary hair and body odor no breast development growth velocity normal No clitoral enlargement; bone age matches age Afebrile · height at the 60th percentile → Reassurance with interval follow-up → isolated hair and odor with normal growth and bone age is premature adrenarche: reassure and follow; nothing points to the axis or the brain, and clitoral enlargement or fast growth would change that
  7. 6-year-old girl has 5 months of pubic hair and severe acne clitoral enlargement linear growth rapidly accelerating No breast budding; no hormone creams or medications at home Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg → Measure 17-hydroxyprogesterone → clitoral enlargement is virilization, which normal adrenarche never causes; it points to an adrenal source, not the axis, so neither a GnRH agonist nor reassurance fits; congenital adrenal hyperplasia shows a high 17-hydroxyprogesterone
  8. 7-year-old boy has pubic hair and acne testes remain prepubertal in size growing faster than his classmates No headache or visual change; no hormone creams at home Afebrile · BP 104/66 mm Hg → Evaluate for a peripheral androgen source → androgen signs with small testes mean the testes are not being driven: a peripheral source, which a GnRH agonist cannot suppress; bilateral testicular enlargement would indicate a central cause
  9. 4-year-old girl is evaluated after a femoral fracture one large hyperpigmented macule with an irregular border free thyroxine high, thyroid-stimulating hormone suppressed No goiter or eye findings noted Afebrile · heart rate 128/min → McCune-Albright syndrome → the mutation is organ-agnostic: any endocrine organ carrying it can secrete autonomously, here the thyroid; Graves disease would not explain the irregular macule and fracture, and neurofibromatosis macules are six or more and smooth, usually with freckling
  10. 7-year-old girl has 6 months of breast development and pubic hair height crossing percentiles upward bone age advanced Skin normal; no headache or visual change Afebrile · BP 100/60 mm Hg → LH response to GnRH stimulation → a rise in LH after GnRH stimulation means the axis is driving it (central); a flat LH points to a peripheral source; estradiol alone cannot tell which axis, and bone age shows progression, not its source
  11. 7-year-old girl was diagnosed with McCune-Albright syndrome last year breast development progressing basal LH prepubertal; one large irregular macule over the right flank Parents ask about treatment for the early puberty Afebrile · bone age advanced → GnRH agonist → the axis is not the driver, so a GnRH agonist does nothing; treat the source, here with aromatase inhibitors or estrogen-receptor blockade
  12. 6-year-old girl has 4 months of pubic hair, acne and clitoral enlargement no breast development 17-hydroxyprogesterone normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate markedly high, testosterone normal No hormone creams or medications at home Afebrile · BP 108/70 mm Hg → Computed tomography of the adrenal glands → a markedly high adrenal androgen with normal testosterone is an adrenal tumor until proven otherwise: image the adrenals, not the brain; normal testosterone points away from the ovary; histology, not labs, separates adenoma from carcinoma
  13. 12-year-old girl is seen for a well visit breast tissue extends beyond the areola without a separate contour pubic hair curled, spread partially across the pubis Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile → Stage 3 → one contour is 3, a second mound is 4; curled hair is past 2, partial spread is below 4; both agree, so one number is acceptable, and it is normal for age
  14. 13-year-old girl is seen for a well visit areola and papilla form a secondary mound above the breast contour adult-type pubic hair that spares the medial thighs Afebrile · height at the 40th percentile → Stage 4 → a second mound is the stage 4 tell; stage 5 needs the areola to recede and hair on the thighs; menarche typically occurs at this stage
  15. 10-year-old girl is seen for a well visit small mound of breast beneath a widened areola a few straight, lightly pigmented hairs along the labia Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile → Stage 2 → a bud and straight hair are stage 2: thelarche, the first sign in girls, at a normal age; curled hair would make it 3
  16. 13-year-old girl is seen for a well visit her first menstrual period began last month breast development began about 2 years ago Her mother asks how much taller she will grow Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile → SMR 4 → menarche comes at SMR 4, about 6 months after peak height velocity (SMR 2 to 3 in girls), so little growth is left
  17. 13-year-old girl is brought in because she has no breast development short stature webbed neck and widely spaced nipples No headaches or visual change Afebrile · height below the 3rd percentile → Obtain a karyotype → no breast development by 13 is delayed puberty, and the dysmorphic features point to Turner syndrome: a karyotype, which a bone age or waiting would miss
  18. 13-year-old boy has tender lumps beneath both nipples 2 cm of subareolar breast tissue on each side sexual maturity rating 3 pubic hair and genitals Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · growing fast this year → Reassurance and follow-up → pubertal gynecomastia is normal at SMR 3 to 4 and coincides with peak height velocity; it resolves within 1 to 2 years, so reassure rather than image
How NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) framed it: question 1

10-year-old girl with 6 months of increased facial hair growth and facial acne At the 50th percentile for height and weight T 37 °C · pulse 64/min · respirations 12/min · BP 110/60 mm Hg mild clitoral enlargement; early male pubic hair pattern serum testosterone 0.2 nmol/L (normal 0.17 to 0.7) dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate 9 μg/mL (normal 0.5 to 5.4); urine 17-ketosteroids 20 mg/24 h (normal 6 to 15) pelvic ultrasonography: no abnormalities

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Androgen insensitivity syndrome: an androgen disorder in a genital-examination stem; but it is a receptor defect in a genetically male child with no androgen effect, so it cannot virilize.
  • Pituitary adenoma: the third adenoma, and a pituitary cause of early puberty; but there is no headache or visual field loss, and pituitary adenomas rarely virilize.
  • Polycystic ovarian syndrome: hirsutism and acne; but testosterone and ovaries are normal, weight is at the 50th percentile, and it does not enlarge the clitoris.

Down to two: adrenal adenoma or ovarian adenoma. Adrenal adenoma: DHEAS comes almost only from the adrenal, and testosterone in a girl mostly from the ovary; a high DHEAS and 17-ketosteroids with normal testosterone and a normal pelvic ultrasound localize the source to the adrenal. An ovarian tumor would raise testosterone. Three options are adenomas at different glands, so it is a location question; at 10, pubic hair alone would be ordinary, and the clitoral enlargement is what makes it virilization.

Decoys Precocity is a complaint, not a diagnosis: sort central from peripheral, then look outside the endocrine system. Fractures in a preschooler: not incidental, one of the triad. No headache, emesis or visual change: nothing intracranial. Stage 4: the adjacent stage the stem negates (no second mound). Enlarged areola: in stage 2, but stage 2 hair is straight.
Pairs with Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth: is bone age ahead of, matching, or behind the age? Inherited Tumor Syndromes: café-au-lait macules from the tumor side.
Transferable rule

When staging, find the phrase that fits exactly one level. When every option is a syndrome sharing the complaint, find the finding only one produces.
