Inherited Tumor Syndromes

the visible lesion and organ pattern name the syndrome · von Hippel-Lindau · neurofibromatosis type 1 · tuberous sclerosisWhat exactly is the retinal lesion, what color is the skin patch, and how many patches are there?

Source vignette Pt — 16 yo M, bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, mother had an adrenal tumor resected, one light brown facial patch without freckling · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1 and Sturge-Weber syndrome
The decision point

Bilateral retinal hemangioblastoma points to von Hippel-Lindau, because no other listed syndrome produces one. NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) gives optic gliomas and Lisch nodules. MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) gives conjunctival and corneal neuromas. Sturge-Weber gives a leptomeningeal and choroidal vascular malformation. Li-Fraumeni gives sarcomas with no characteristic eye finding. The mother's resected adrenal tumor reads as a pheochromocytoma transmitted in autosomal dominant fashion. Hemangioblastoma plus adrenal medullary tumor is the von Hippel-Lindau organ pattern, with clear cell renal carcinoma the third member. A single light brown facial macule is a normal café-au-lait spot. It is not the multiple macules of NF1 and not a red-purple port-wine stain.

Consider a teenager found confused after an unwitnessed fall. A fibroma growing from under a toenail and calcified nodules lining the lateral ventricles on CT (computed tomography) indicate tuberous sclerosis complex. The fall was a seizure, and the nodules are subependymal hamartomas. The nail lesion is a periungual fibroma, which appears in adolescence. NF1 puts neurofibromas on the trunk and a glioma on the optic nerve. Ataxia-telangiectasia starts with ataxia in early childhood. The nail-bed sign of endocarditis is a splinter hemorrhage, not a fibroma.

Defining criteria The VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) testing gate — any patient with a retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma undergoes VHL gene testing, family history or not · The café-au-lait gate — an isolated macule is normal; six or more with regular borders plus axillary freckling is NF1 (each macule over 5 mm before puberty or over 15 mm after puberty); macules with jagged, irregular borders that usually respect the midline and follow the lines of Blaschko suggest McCune-Albright. Count, border, distribution and freckling are four separate criteria, and the exam varies whichever one is not being checked · Patch color as a criterion — Sturge-Weber's lesion is a red-purple vascular port-wine stain; a light brown patch is pigmented and belongs to a different family
Pertinent positives & negatives Bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas — essentially syndrome-defining; retinal hemangioblastoma may be the first neoplasm of VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) and by itself triggers gene testing · Mother's adrenal tumor removed — pheochromocytoma in a first-degree relative; autosomal dominant transmission, and the second organ of the VHL pattern · A single light brown 4-cm patch — one café-au-lait macule, a normal finding, lacking the multiplicity of NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and the color of Sturge-Weber · Age 16 with painless progressive blurring — VHL can present at any age but usually presents in early adulthood. Vision falls from retinal edema and distortion · Blood pressure 110/72 mm Hg and an otherwise normal examination — no clinically active pheochromocytoma today, which does not exclude one and is why surveillance is needed
Inherited tumor syndromes: the differential
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) tellExcluded here by
Von Hippel-LindauAutosomal dominant loss of the VHL tumor suppressor on chromosome 3; tumors of retina, central nervous system, adrenal medulla and kidneyRetinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, clear cell renal carcinoma(the answer)
Neurofibromatosis type 1Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder of skin, nerve and eyeMultiple café-au-lait macules with axillary freckling; cutaneous neurofibromas on the trunk; optic glioma and Lisch nodules; seizures in someOne macule only, which is normal; the retinal lesion is a hemangioblastoma
Sturge-Weber syndromeLeptomeningeal and ocular capillary-venous malformationRed-purple port-wine stain, seizures, glaucomaThe patch is light brown and pigmented, not vascular
Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2BRET proto-oncogene; medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytomaConjunctival or corneal neuromas, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitusEye lesion is a hemangioblastoma; no thyroid disease
Li-Fraumeni syndromeAutosomal dominant TP53 loss; many tumor types across a young familySoft tissue sarcoma, early breast cancer, adrenocortical carcinoma; no characteristic eye or skin lesionNo hemangioblastoma belongs to it
Tuberous sclerosis complexAutosomal dominant TSC1 or TSC2 mutation, inherited or new; benign hamartomas of brain, eye, skin, heart and kidney; epilepsy in most, intellectual disability and autismAsh-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas; calcified subependymal nodules on CT; cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipomaNo skin hamartoma here, and its brain lesions are nodules and tubers, not hemangioblastomas
Neurofibromatosis type 2Autosomal dominant tumors of nerve sheath and meningesBilateral vestibular schwannomasThe eighth nerve, not the retina
Management, in one line Confirm with VHL gene testing (VHL: von Hippel-Lindau). Then begin lifelong surveillance: retinal examination, plasma or urine metanephrines, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of brain and spine, and MRI of abdomen. Resect tumors as they appear. For the retinal lesions, laser therapy is the preferred treatment.
Tuberous sclerosis complex Skin — hypopigmented ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas over the cheeks and nose, a shagreen patch (orange-peel plaque on the lower back), and periungual fibromas, which appear in adolescence or adulthood · Brain — subependymal nodules, calcified on CT along the ventricles; cortical tubers, best seen on MRI; a nodule can grow into a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma that obstructs CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) flow and causes hydrocephalus, which needs resection · Seizures — epilepsy in most, often infantile spasms, but the first seizure can come at any age, adolescence included; intellectual disability, autism and behavior disorders · Heart and kidney — cardiac rhabdomyoma; renal angiomyolipoma · Surveillance — skin and eye exams, serial MRI of brain and kidneys, baseline echocardiogram and serial ECGs (electrocardiograms), baseline EEG (electroencephalogram), and neuropsychiatric screening · Not tuberous sclerosis — NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1): café-au-lait macules, trunk neurofibromas, optic glioma; VHL (von Hippel-Lindau): cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas; ataxia-telangiectasia: ataxia from early childhood, poorly coordinated eye movements, conjunctival telangiectasias; endocarditis: fever, murmur and splinter hemorrhages
Neurofibromatosis type 1: tumor risk Optic nerve glioma — the most common brain tumor in neurofibromatosis type 1; usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma of one or both optic nerves or the chiasm · Presentation — insidious vision loss, proptosis and optic atrophy · Eye surveillance — children with neurofibromatosis type 1 need an eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18 · Pheochromocytoma — risk also raised · No established link — medulloblastoma, craniopharyngioma, and arteriovenous malformation, which belongs to Wyburn-Mason syndrome
Decision spine Name the retinal lesion exactly. — Hemangioblastoma → VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) · If it is a different eye lesion: — optic glioma or Lisch nodules point to NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1). Conjunctival neuromas point to MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B). Glaucoma with a choroidal malformation points to Sturge-Weber · Read the skin patch's color. — Light brown pigmented = café-au-lait; red-purple vascular = port-wine · Count the skin lesions. — One café-au-lait macule is normal; multiple plus axillary freckling is NF1 · Read the family's tumor for its organ. — Adrenal medulla with kidney and CNS (central nervous system) points to VHL. Adrenal medulla with thyroid points to MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2)
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Dilated retinal examinationFirstRetinal hemangioblastomaVon Hippel-Lindau suspected, with or without a family history
VHL gene testingConfirmsPathogenic VHL variantVHL disease; offer testing to first-degree relatives now
Plasma or urine metanephrinesStagingElevated metanephrinesPheochromocytoma: alpha blockade before beta blockade, then resection
MRI of brain and spineStagingCerebellar or spinal hemangioblastomaCNS tumors of VHL
MRI of abdomenStagingEnhancing renal massClear cell carcinoma: nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy
Noncontrast head CT after a first seizureBy branchCalcified subependymal nodules along the ventriclesTuberous sclerosis complex; brain MRI shows cortical tubers
Whole-body PET (positron emission tomography) imagingSkipAdds nothing to gene testing and targeted MRIVHL testing follows the lesion; surveillance covers the four organs
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M with bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, a mother who had an adrenal tumor resected, and one light brown facial patch → Von Hippel-Lindau disease → The eye lesion names the syndrome
  2. 34 yo M with a solitary cerebellar hemangioblastoma and no family history of tumors → VHL gene testing → Testing follows the lesion, not the pedigree
  3. Patient with newly confirmed von Hippel-Lindau disease → Retinal, adrenal, neuraxis and abdominal surveillance→ retinal examination, plasma metanephrines, MRI of brain and spine, and MRI of abdomen; The four organs the syndrome occupies
  4. 22 yo F newly diagnosed with von Hippel-Lindau disease who has an asymptomatic 15-year-old brother → Offer him VHL gene testing now → each first-degree relative carries a 50% risk, and surveillance starts in childhood
  5. 40 yo M with von Hippel-Lindau disease and a 3 cm enhancing renal mass → Nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy → Clear cell carcinoma, with more lesions expected
  6. 28 yo F with von Hippel-Lindau disease, an adrenal mass and elevated metanephrines, scheduled for resection → Alpha blockade started before any beta blockade → Unopposed alpha stimulation otherwise
  7. 4-month-old with a red-purple patch over the V1 distribution and a focal seizure → Brain MRI and ophthalmology referral→ for a leptomeningeal angioma and for glaucoma screening; Sturge-Weber syndrome
  8. 7-year-old with 8 cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules and an optic glioma → Neurofibromatosis type 1 → Multiplicity is the criterion, not presence
  9. 24-year-old with medullary thyroid carcinoma, a pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas of the lips and a marfanoid habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B → Neuromas rather than hemangioblastomas
  10. The molecular defect underlying von Hippel-Lindau disease → Loss of a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3 → Autosomal dominant inheritance
  11. 9 year old with painless firm rubbery tongue nodules, marfanoid habitus and long fingers → Medullary thyroid carcinoma → MEN2B: aggressive and early; prophylactic thyroidectomy before age 1 year
  12. Child with newly diagnosed MEN2B; what else must be evaluated → Plasma fractionated metanephrines → About half have pheochromocytoma
  13. Adult with primary hyperparathyroidism, a prolactinoma and a gastrinoma → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 → No marfanoid habitus and no mucosal neuromas
  14. Patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and parathyroid hyperplasia, with a normal habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A → Parathyroid rather than neuromas separates 2A from 2B
  15. Child with perioral pigmented macules and recurrent intussusception → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → Pigmented macules, not neuromas; the risk is polyps and cancer
  16. Adult with recurrent epistaxis and ruby mucosal papules that blanch with pressure → Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia → Telangiectasias blanch; neuromas do not
  17. Newborn with bilateral absence of the iris, hypospadias and an undescended left testis → Wilms tumor → WAGR (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, range of developmental delay): abdominal ultrasonography every 3 months until about age 5 to 8 years
  18. Newborn with aniridia and genitourinary anomalies; the underlying lesion → An 11p13 deletion → WAGR: Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary, Range of developmental delay
  19. Why Wilms tumor in WAGR differs from isolated Wilms tumor → It is often bilateral and presents earlier → Isolated disease is usually unilateral at age 2 to 5
  20. Macrosomic newborn with macroglossia and hemihyperplasia at risk for embryonal tumors → Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome → Overgrowth rather than aniridia
  21. 17 yo M found confused at the bottom of the stairs after an unwitnessed fall, most likely a seizure; 2-cm forehead contusion; a firm flesh-colored fibroma growing from beneath a toenail; head CT shows calcified nodules along the walls of the lateral ventricles → Tuberous sclerosis complex → Periungual fibroma plus calcified subependymal nodules; surveillance of brain, kidney, heart, eyes and skin
  22. 8 yo F newly diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex after a first seizure, with ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas; normal blood pressure and development so far → Brain and kidney MRI, echocardiogram and ECG, EEG, and skin and eye exams → Surveillance follows the organs the hamartomas occupy, plus neuropsychiatric screening
  23. Asymptomatic 17 yo M at a sports physical with about 10 light brown macules 0.6 to 2 cm across the trunk and limbs and freckling in both axillae → Optic nerve glioma → Neurofibromatosis type 1; eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18
  24. 6-year-old with 7 café-au-lait macules over 5 mm, inguinal freckling, normal vision and a normal examination otherwise → Yearly eye examination → Neurofibromatosis type 1; screens for optic nerve glioma
  25. 9-year-old with neurofibromatosis type 1 and months of painless vision loss in one eye, mild proptosis and a pale optic disc → Optic nerve glioma → Usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma
Decoy note The skin patch drew nearly two in five readers: 20% chose NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and 18% chose Sturge-Weber. A solitary café-au-lait macule is normal, so this most conspicuous physical finding does not discriminate. The mother's adrenal tumor supplies both the inheritance pattern and the second organ. The normal blood pressure does not help the diagnosis, but it indicates that no pheochromocytoma is active yet.
Pearls Retinal hemangioblastoma is von Hippel-Lindau until gene testing says otherwise; the pheochromocytoma and clear cell renal carcinoma follow. · A retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma by itself warrants referral to genetics. VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) testing follows the lesion, with or without a family history. · Eye lesions by syndrome: hemangioblastoma → VHL · optic glioma with Lisch nodules → NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) · conjunctival and corneal neuromas → MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) · choroidal malformation with glaucoma → Sturge-Weber. · Read a patch's color, not merely its presence. Light brown pigmented is café-au-lait, red-purple vascular is port-wine, and they belong to different syndromes. · VHL surveillance covers its organs: retina, brain and spine, adrenal medulla and kidney. The follow-up is therefore an eye exam, metanephrines, and two MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans. · Up to 35% of pheochromocytomas may be germline, so genetic testing should be considered for every patient; a younger age at presentation or bilateral tumors make a hereditary syndrome more likely. The syndromes include VHL, MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), NF1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene variants. · Before resecting a pheochromocytoma, alpha blockade precedes beta blockade; reversing the order leaves alpha stimulation unopposed. · How NBME framed it: a well 17-year-old at a sports physical has about 10 light brown macules and axillary freckling, and the syndrome is never named. After puberty only macules over 15 mm count, so the axillary freckling supplies the second criterion. The lead-in asks which lesion carries a raised risk compared with the general population.
Pairs with Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers pheochromocytoma from the blood-pressure side, reaching the same tumor from a different complaint. Ask: is the pheochromocytoma isolated, or is it one organ of a syndrome? Related conditions without their own brief: the neurocutaneous syndromes as a set, namely NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1), NF2 (neurofibromatosis type 2), tuberous sclerosis and Sturge-Weber. Part I Puberty covers the border and distribution attributes of café-au-lait macules. Part II Abdominal Mass in a Young Child covers the mass itself. Ask: is it within the kidney, and is the child older than 2? Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers ataxia-telangiectasia and its infections. Ask: is the skin lesion vascular, or a fibrous tumor? Part I Brain Tumors in a Child covers optic pathway glioma and craniopharyngioma as masses. Ask: does the visual field loss come from the optic nerve or from the sella?
Transferable rule When a visible lesion identifies a syndrome, the lesion's category is shared across syndromes, but its identity is not. Name the tissue and the color before matching. The most conspicuous physical finding may be the one that does not discriminate.
Unchecked attributeNeurofibromatosis type 1, for two café-au-lait macules: Two macules sit between the isolated-is-normal rule and the six of NF1. A count rule alone therefore lands on NF1. The border, the distribution that respects the midline and the absent freckling all argue against it.
Salient decoyNeurofibromatosis type 1: One macule is normal; NF1 requires multiple with axillary freckling, and its eye lesions are optic glioma and Lisch nodules, never a hemangioblastoma
Unchecked attributeSturge-Weber syndrome: The patch is the wrong kind; port-wine stains are red-purple vascular malformations, and this one is light brown and pigmented
True-fact-wrong-slotLi-Fraumeni syndrome: TP53 disease is sarcomas, early breast and adrenocortical carcinoma, with no characteristic eye or skin lesion and no hemangioblastoma
Class-vs-memberMultiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B: Its eye findings are conjunctival and corneal neuromas, and it brings medullary thyroid carcinoma, which nobody in this stem has
Class-vs-memberNeurofibromatosis type 1, for the teenager with the toenail fibroma: Also autosomal dominant with seizures, but its skin tumors are neurofibromas on the trunk and its brain tumor is an optic glioma; calcified subependymal nodules belong to tuberous sclerosis
Unchecked attributeAtaxia-telangiectasia: Autosomal recessive, with ataxia from early childhood and vascular telangiectasias rather than a fibrous nail tumor, and no ventricular nodules
Salient decoyBacterial endocarditis: The nail finding pulls toward it, but endocarditis gives splinter hemorrhages with fever and a murmur, not a firm periungual fibroma
Salient decoyMedulloblastoma, for the teenager with 10 café-au-lait macules: The most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, with raised intracranial pressure and ataxia, but neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotCraniopharyngioma: A Rathke pouch remnant that causes bitemporal field loss; neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotArteriovenous malformation: Retinal and midbrain arteriovenous malformations belong to Wyburn-Mason syndrome, not neurofibromatosis type 1
True-fact-wrong-slotCerebral aneurysm: An adult cause of intracranial hemorrhage; the tumor this skin pattern predicts is an optic nerve glioma
